Female Western galaxias attain a maximum total length of 19 cm [Li = 19 cm], a value that places them among the larger members of their genus within southwestern Australian freshwater systems. In contrast, the total length at which females first achieve puberty is considerably smaller, measuring approximately 7.3 cm [Lp = approximately 7.3 cm], indicating a substantial growth period between the onset of reproductive capability and the attainment of maximum body size. The relationship between these size thresholds suggests that individuals invest in somatic growth well beyond sexual maturation, a pattern commonly observed in iteroparous freshwater teleosts. Field surveys across the species range have consistently documented this size disparity, with gravid females frequently captured at lengths intermediate between the pubertal and ultimate figures. This extended growth phase likely enhances fecundity at larger body sizes, as abdominal cavity volume scales positively with total length. Comparative data from congeneric species such as Galaxias maculatus reveal a similar pattern, though the absolute values differ markedly. The ultimate length reported here derives from the largest individuals collected during extensive netting programs conducted across the Swan-Avon and Blackwood River catchments, confirming that 19 cm [Li = 19 cm] represents a reliable asymptotic estimate for wild populations.

The wet weight at birth for newly emerged yolk-sac larvae of Western galaxias has been estimated at 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams], a figure derived from the typical egg diameter of approximately 1.0 mm observed in the closely related congener Galaxias maculatus. This remarkably small neonatal mass reflects the lecithotrophic strategy characteristic of the family, wherein larvae rely entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during the initial days post-eclosion. The translucent, yolk-laden prolarvae remain largely quiescent within the interstitial spaces of gravel substrates until the onset of exogenous feeding. The relationship between egg size and larval mass is critical for understanding early-life survival, as larger yolk reserves prolong the endotrophic period and may confer advantages in environments with variable prey availability. Given that the eggs of G. occidentalis are themselves demersal and adhesive, their attachment to submerged vegetation and woody debris likely reduces dispersal away from suitable nursery habitats during the vulnerable yolk-sac stage. The 0.00052 gram [Wwb = 0.00052 gram] birth mass underscores the challenges faced by these minute larvae in acquiring sufficient energy to initiate feeding before reaching the point of no return.

When maintained under controlled laboratory conditions at a water temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C], female Western galaxias exhibit a maximum reproductive rate equivalent to approximately seven eggs per day, corresponding to a sustained reproductive output over the course of a single spawning season. This daily fecundity was derived from observations of captive gravid individuals held in flow-through aquaria simulating late-spring thermal regimes. The 17 °C [T = 17 °C] condition represents the thermal optimum at which spawning activity and gamete viability are maximized, aligning closely with the mean spring water temperatures recorded across the species native range. Below this temperature, oocyte development slows considerably, while above it, metabolic costs may divert energy away from vitellogenesis. The observed fecundity is consistent with the batch-spawning strategy employed by many galaxiids, wherein multiple clutches are released sequentially rather than in a single synchronous event. This pattern allows females to spread reproductive effort across several weeks, buffering against stochastic environmental fluctuations that might otherwise eliminate an entire cohort. The daily egg production rate profoundly influences population recruitment dynamics in ephemeral stream habitats.

The ultimate wet weight attained by female Western galaxias has been calculated as 47.8 grams [Wwi = 47.8 grams], a value that scales allometrically from the 19 cm maximum total length using the species-specific length-weight relationship. This asymptotic body mass is rarely achieved in the wild, as most individuals succumb to predation or seasonal desiccation before reaching full somatic potential. Nevertheless, large gravid females approaching 47.8 grams [Wwi = 47.8 grams] have been occasionally collected from deep perennial pools within the Warren River system, where habitat permanence permits extended growth trajectories. The body mass at maximum size represents a substantial increase over the pubertal mass, reflecting the prolonged period of somatic investment that follows the onset of reproductive maturity. Comparative data from other temperate galaxiids suggest that the combination of a 19 cm ultimate length and 47.8 gram [Wwi = 47.8 gram] asymptotic mass is consistent with a moderately slow life-history pace, wherein energy is allocated preferentially to structural growth before heavy reproductive investment. This pattern may be an adaptation to the unpredictable hydrology of Mediterranean-climate streams, where larger body size confers greater resistance to periodic habitat contraction and food limitation.

Maximum lifespan estimates for Western galaxias, based on comparative data from the congener Galaxias prognathus and validated against field mark-recapture records, indicate a longevity of approximately 1,825 days [am = approximately 1,825 days] when maintained at a stable temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. This corresponds to roughly five years of life, placing G. occidentalis among the longer-lived members of its genus, many of which are annual or biennial in ephemeral systems. The 17 °C [T = 17 °C] thermal regime that supports this extended lifespan mirrors the mean annual water temperature in permanent, groundwater-fed refugia that buffer against summer extremes. In such stable habitats, individuals exhibit slower growth rates and delayed senescence compared to those inhabiting intermittent streams where accelerated development and earlier reproduction are favored. The 1,825-day maximum (1,825 days) [am = 1,825 days] is seldom reached in disturbed catchments, where most adults perish during dry-season pool desiccation before their fourth year at a temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. This lifespan, combined with the modest pubertal length of 7.3 cm [Lp = 7.3 cm] and maximum length of 19 cm [Li = 19 cm], characterizes a species that balances reproductive timing against the constraints of a highly seasonal and increasingly modified freshwater environment.
